paragraphs: “Captain, stop it. A brave man has to hold himself together,” Kolya muttered.
“You’ll ruin the flowers,” said Alyosha. “And Mamma is waiting for them. She’s sitting there crying because you wouldn’t give her any before. Ilusha’s little bed is still there—”

“Yes, yes, Mamma!” Snegiryov suddenly remembered. “They’ll take the bed away, they’ll take it away,” he added, as if afraid they really would. He jumped up and ran for home again. But it was not far, and they all got there together. Snegiryov opened the door in a rush and called out to his wife, the same woman he had quarreled with so cruelly only a little while earlier:

“Mamma, my poor crippled darling, Ilusha has sent you these flowers,” he cried, holding out a little bunch that had been frozen and broken while he struggled in the snow. But at that moment he saw Ilusha’s little boots in the corner by the bed, where the landlady had set them neatly side by side. At the sight of the old, patched, rusty-looking, stiff boots he threw up his hands and rushed to them. He fell on his knees, snatched up one boot, pressed his lips to it and began kissing it greedily, crying, “Ilusha, old man, dear old man, where are your little feet?”

“Where have you taken him? Where have you taken him?” the madwoman cried in a heartbreaking voice. Nina, too, burst into sobs. Kolya ran out of the room, and the boys followed him. At last Alyosha went out too.
“Let them cry,” he said to Kolya. “Trying to comfort them now won’t help. We’ll wait a minute and then go back in.”

“No, it’s no use, it’s awful,” Kolya agreed. “Do you know, Karamazov,” he lowered his voice so that no one could hear, “I feel terribly sad. If it were only possible to bring him back, I’d give anything in the world to do it.”
“Ah, so would I,” said Alyosha.
“What do you think, Karamazov? Should we come back here tonight? He’ll be drunk, you know.”

“Perhaps he will. Let’s come together, you and I. That will be enough, to spend an hour with them, with the mother and Nina. If we all come together, we’ll remind them of everything again,” Alyosha suggested.
“The landlady is laying the table for them now. There’ll be a funeral dinner or something, and the priest is coming. Shall we go back for it, Karamazov?”
“Of course,” said Alyosha.
“It’s all so strange, Karamazov. Such sorrow, and then pancakes after it. It all seems so unnatural in our religion.”
“They’re going to have salmon, too,” the boy who had found out about Troy said in a loud voice.

“I earnestly ask you, Kartashov, not to interrupt again with your idiotic remarks, especially when nobody is talking to you and nobody cares whether you exist or not!” Kolya snapped irritably. The boy turned crimson but did not dare to answer.
Meanwhile they were strolling slowly along the path, and suddenly Smurov exclaimed:
“There’s Ilusha’s stone, the one they wanted to bury him under.”

They all stopped by the big stone. Alyosha looked at it, and the whole picture of what Snegiryov had told him that day rose at once before his imagination: how Ilusha, weeping and hugging his father, had cried, “Father, father, how he insulted you!”
Something seemed to seize his soul all at once. Serious and earnest, he looked from one to another of the bright, pleasant faces of Ilusha’s schoolmates, and then said to them:
“Boys, I’d like to say a word to you, here in this place.”
The boys gathered round him and at once fixed attentive, expectant eyes on him.

“Boys, we shall soon part. For a while I’ll be with my two brothers. One is going to Siberia, and the other is lying at death’s door. But soon I’ll leave this town, perhaps for a long time, so we’ll part. Let’s make a pact here, at Ilusha’s stone, that we will never forget Ilusha, or one another. And whatever happens to us later in life, even if we don’t meet for twenty years, let’s always remember how we buried the poor boy we once threw stones at, do you remember, by the bridge? And afterwards we all grew so fond of him. He was a fine boy, kind-hearted and brave. He cared about his father’s honor, he was hurt by the cruel insult to it, and he stood up for him. So, first of all, boys, we will remember him all our lives. Even if we’re busy with the most important matters, even if we win great honor or fall into terrible misfortune, let’s still remember how good it was here once, when we were all together, joined by a good and kind feeling. For the time we loved that poor boy, it made us better, perhaps, than we really are. My little doves—let me call you that, because you look very like them, those pretty blue birds, at this moment as I look at your good dear faces. My dear children, perhaps you won’t understand what I’m saying to you, because I often speak very unclearly, but you’ll remember it all the same, and some day you’ll agree with my words. You must know that there is nothing higher or stronger or healthier or better for life in the future than some good memory, especially a memory of childhood, of home. People talk to you a great deal about your education. But some good, sacred memory, kept from childhood, is perhaps the best education there is. If a man takes many such memories with him into life, he is safe to the end of his days. And even if only one good memory is left in our hearts, it may save us someday. We may even grow wicked later on. We may be unable to hold back from a bad action, may laugh at men’s tears, and at people who say, as Kolya did just now, ‘I want to suffer for all men,’ and may even jeer spitefully at such people. But however bad we may become—which God forbid—when we remember how we buried Ilusha, how we loved him in his last days, and how we have been talking like friends all together at this stone, the cruelest and most mocking of us, if we do become so, will not dare to laugh inwardly at having been kind and good at this moment! What’s more, perhaps that one memory may keep him from great evil, and he will stop and say, ‘Yes, I was good and brave and honest then!’ Let him laugh to himself, that doesn’t matter. A man often laughs at what’s good and kind. That’s only from thoughtlessness. But I assure you, boys, that as he laughs he will say at once in his heart, ‘No, I’m wrong to laugh, because that’s not a thing to laugh at.’”
“That will be so, I understand you, Karamazov!” cried Kolya, his eyes flashing.
The boys were excited and wanted to say something too, but they held back, watching the speaker intently and with deep feeling.

“I say this in case we become bad,” Alyosha went on, “but there’s no reason why we should become bad, is there, boys? Let’s be, first and above all, kind, then honest, and then let’s never forget each other! I say that again. For my part I give you my word that I’ll never forget a single one of you. Every face looking at me now I’ll remember, even thirty years from now. Just now Kolya said to Kartashov that we didn’t care whether he exists or not. But I can’t forget that Kartashov exists, and that he isn’t blushing now as he did when he found out who founded Troy, but is looking at me with his jolly, kind, dear little eyes. Boys, my dear boys, let’s all be generous and brave like Ilusha, clever, brave and generous like Kolya (though he’ll be ever so much cleverer when he’s grown up), and let’s all be as modest, as clever and as sweet as Kartashov. But why am I talking about those two? You are all dear to me, boys, from this day on. I have a place in my heart for every one of you, and I ask you to keep a place in your hearts for me! Well, and who has united us in this kind, good feeling which we shall remember and mean to remember all our lives? Who, if not Ilusha, the good boy, the dear boy, precious to us for ever! Let’s never forget him. May his memory live for ever in our hearts from this time on!”
“Yes, yes, for ever, for ever!” the boys cried in their ringing voices, their faces softened.
“Let’s remember his face, his clothes, his poor little boots, his coffin, his unhappy, sinful father, and how boldly he stood up for him, alone against the whole school.”
“We’ll remember, we’ll remember,” cried the boys. “He was brave, he was good!”
“Ah, how I loved him!” exclaimed Kolya.
“Ah, children, ah, dear friends, don’t be afraid of life! Life is so good when you do something good and just!”
“Yes, yes,” the boys repeated eagerly.
“Karamazov, we love you!” a voice, probably Kartashov’s, cried out impulsively.
“We love you, we love you!” they all echoed. Many of them had tears in their eyes.
“Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya shouted in ecstasy.
“And may the dead boy’s memory live for ever!” Alyosha added again, with feeling.
“For ever!” the boys chimed in again.
“Karamazov,” cried Kolya, “can it be true, what they teach us in religion, that we shall all rise from the dead and live and see each other again, all of us, Ilusha too?”
“Of course we’ll all rise again. Of course we’ll see each other, and we’ll tell each other, with joy and gladness, everything that has happened!” Alyosha answered, half laughing, half carried away.
“Ah, how splendid it will be!” broke from Kolya.

“Well, now we’ll finish talking and go to his funeral dinner. Don’t be put off by our eating pancakes—it’s a very old custom, and there’s something nice in it!” laughed Alyosha. “Well, let’s go! And now we go hand in hand.”
“And always like this, all our lives, hand in hand! Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya cried once more, rapturously, and once more the boys took up his cry: “Hurrah for Karamazov!”
THE END
